newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Ousted Afghan leader in neighbouring Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Afghan leader in neighbouring Tajikistan.

text.p: Ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani is in neighbouring Tajikistan after the Taleban militia took the northern Afghan town of Mazar-i-Sharif last week, an official close to Rabbani said on Monday.

"Rabbani and several members of his cabinet are now in the town of Kulyab in Tajikistan's south," the source told Reuters by telephone from the Tajik capital Dushanbe, but gave no date of Rabbani's arrival.
Rabbani was driven from the Afghan capital Kabul by the purist Islamic Taleban militia last September.
The official told Reuters that Rabbani's military chief, Ahmad Shah Masood, was now holed up in the Panjsher Valley in northern Afghnistan but gave no further details.

General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who is an ethnic Uzbek and the other half of the beleaguered anti-Taleban alliance, is in Turkey after he was driven out of Mazar-i-Sharif and several other major towns by the Taleban at the weekend.
The source added hundreds of refugees had begun to arrive in the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan.
"So far several hundred Afghan refugees have arrived in Kulyab...As for northern Afghanistan, in many regions locals hailed the advance of the Taleban and raised its white flags," the source said.

Tajikistan and the other ex-Soviet states of Central Asia have voiced fears that militant, Taleban-style Islam could spread northwards across their borders. Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan all share borders with the war ravaged state.
Tajikistan's defence and security ministries held an urgent meeting at the weekend, discussing measures to reinforce the Afghan border and prevent a massive influx of refugees.
The republic is itself reeling from a bitter four-year civil war. A fragile peace secured last December is often rattled by maverick armed bands and drug traders acting out of bases in Afghanistan.
Russia, which is separated from Afghanistan by more than 1,000 km (600 miles) of Central Asian territory, has about 20,000 troops stationed in Tajikistan.
They guard the republic's remote, mountainous border with Afghanistan and view themselves as a shield against Islamic fundamentalism.
A statement issued by Uzbekistan's foreign ministry on Sunday said that Uzbek border troops were "taking measures to reinforce the Afghan border to exclude any provocations".
In Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov has warned the Taleban not to violate the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a loose grouping of 12 ex-Soviet states.
"(Any infringement) will provoke very tough and effective actions from the CIS side," Interfax news agency quoted Primakov as saying on Sunday.
